## Context

The Reference Architectures Workstream now has a job-oriented foundation for a Reference Architecture knowledge-base, which can grow as contributors add and validate new patterns and reference architectures:

```text
Reusable pattern
  - solves one recurring workflow problem
    e.g. durable wait · human approval gate

        ↓ patterns are composed into

Job-oriented reference architectures
  - each combines patterns, capability roles, boundaries, guarantees, and exit states
    for a recognizable practitioner job, e.g. human-approved operation

        ↑ scenarios test whether it fits

Real-world scenario / use case
  - provides evidence from a real workflow
    e.g. invoice processing
```

A recent [specification-driven experiment](https://github.com/aaif/wg-workflows-and-process-integration/pull/21) (PR #21) tested a further idea:

> The Reference Architecture can be something a person or AI **uses** to turn a workflow problem into a reviewable design, rather than only a catalogue of documents to read.


**This issue asks the WG to make two north-star decisions about where the Reference Architecture should go next.** 
Detailed work needed to get there will be decided afterward.

---

## Decision 1: What is the intended end state of the RA?

> Should the long-term RA provide reusable guidance only, or should it also produce a versioned, machine-readable Workflow Design Specification (WDS) for each concrete workflow?

### Option A - the RA ends with reusable guidance

```text
Patterns and reference architectures explain reusable solutions.
A person or organization chooses how to document a particular workflow after applying that guidance.
```

The WG would publish patterns, job-oriented reference architectures, and scenario validation. It would **not** yet say:

> “After applying this guidance, document your specific workflow in this common format.”

People and organizations could use an internal architecture document, a vendor-specific workflow definition, a diagram, a ticket/ADR, a spreadsheet, or no standard artifact.

**Consequence:** The long-term RA remains a human-readable knowledgebase of patterns, job-oriented reference architectures, and scenario validation. It does not need a canonical workflow-design artifact, schema, generated views, or machine-readable handoff model.

### Option B - the RA also produces a versioned, machine-readable Workflow Design Specification

```text
Patterns and reference architectures explain reusable solutions.
The RA also helps a person apply them to one specific workflow and produce a canonical Workflow Design Specification (WDS).
```

The WDS is a versioned, schema-valid, machine-readable source of truth-such as YAML. 
Human-readable artifacts are views of that same design: rationale, architecture and execution diagrams, review material, and implementation handoff.

```text
Reference Architecture knowledgebase

  patterns · reference architectures · principles · shared vocabulary

        ↓
        applied to a specific workflow through an agreed method
        ↓

Canonical Workflow Design Specification (WDS)

  versioned · schema-valid · machine-readable source of truth

        ↓
        rendered or derived as needed
        ↓

Human-readable views

  rationale · diagrams · review material · implementation handoff
```

The method that applies the knowledgebase to a use case, the WDS schema, vocabulary, identifiers, generated views, and repository structure are follow-up design decisions.

This is a north-star decision. Choosing B does not approve a specific schema, vocabulary, identifier set, or generated-view approach; it sets the direction for future, separately reviewed work needed to reach that outcome.

**Consequence:** record the north-star decision in an ADR. If Option B is chosen, future proposals can define the application method, WDS schema/versioning, and human-readable views as separate, reviewable steps.

---

## Decision 2: Which concepts from the specification-driven RA approach ([PR #21](https://github.com/aaif/wg-workflows-and-process-integration/pull/21)) should be brought into the job-oriented foundation?

[PR #21](https://github.com/aaif/wg-workflows-and-process-integration/pull/21) tested a **specification-driven** approach: use the Reference Architecture to turn a workflow problem into a concrete design and its views.

Selecting a concept means it is worth bringing into the job-oriented foundation (will be done through dedicated PRs).

### Candidate concepts - suggested foundation-first order

This is a rough order of dependency, not a claim that every item must be built or voted on in sequence. The early items define the shared building blocks from which later guidance can be composed; the later items apply, package, or map that guidance.

| # | Candidate concept | What it would add | What it means in practice |
|---|---|---|---|
| 1 | Primitive catalog | An explicit RA knowledgebase layer for workflow building blocks used in patterns and architectures. It uses the shared terms agreed by the Taxonomy workstream, then explains how each primitive is used and combined when designing workflow patterns and reference architectures. | A `primitives/` folder or catalog document. Taxonomy defines what terms such as trigger or handoff mean; the RA catalog defines each primitive's workflow behavior, inputs/outputs, state and authority implications, and how patterns/architectures may combine it. |
| 2 | Shared architecture invariants | A small catalog of non-negotiable guarantees that apply across multiple patterns and architectures, so they are stated once and referenced consistently instead of rewritten or weakened in each document. | An `invariants.md` document containing a small set of named rules that patterns and architectures reference instead of redefining. Each rule states what must always hold and which designs it applies to. |
| 3 | Capability-role catalog | An explicit RA knowledgebase layer for logical runtime roles repeatedly required by architectures, such as a state store, controlled effect executor, human interaction surface, and audit or system-of-record role, and what each role must provide. | A `capabilities/` folder or catalog document defining each logical role, the responsibilities and guarantees it must provide, and the boundaries it must preserve. |
| 4 | Stable IDs and registry | A machine-readable index of agreed RA concepts. Stable IDs let names and wording improve without breaking references from patterns, architectures, WDSs, documentation, or tools. | A versioned YAML or JSON registry that maps stable IDs to each agreed concept, name, status, and documentation link. |
| 5 | Examples as acceptance tests | A defined practice for using a small set of contrasting real use cases to test whether the RA is complete and usable, not merely illustrative. | One or two canonical scenario documents with expected design questions or outcomes. New patterns and architectures are tested against them to show whether the guidance fits, exposes a gap, or needs a new composition. |
| 6 | Execution profiles | A reusable way to describe the overall control and authority arrangement of a workflow run, for example whether the workflow, agent, human, event, or external runtime generally directs continuation. | A `profiles/` folder containing short documents for each agreed control and authority arrangement. |
| 7 | Cross-cutting overlays | A reusable way to attach controls that recur across otherwise different architectures, such as durable execution, protected effects, budget limits, or execution history, without copying the same requirements into every pattern. | An `overlays/` folder containing reusable control documents. An architecture declares an overlay when its conditions apply, for example a durable run, protected external effect, budget limit, or execution-history requirement. |
| 8 | Goal-based entry paths | A clear way for users of the RA to enter and navigate it based on what they want to do: design a new workflow, assess an existing one, solve a focused design problem, plan platform capabilities, or evaluate a runtime. | A `how-to-use-the-ra.md` guide that routes each need to the relevant patterns, architectures, design method, assessment guidance, capability guidance, or runtime mappings. |
| 9 | Workflow Design Method | A repeatable method that applies the RA knowledgebase to a concrete use case and produces its WDS. | A short `workflow-design-method.md` that guides a person or AI from a use case through selecting and composing RA guidance to a WDS. |
| 10 | Machine-readable WDS | The versioned, schema-valid canonical design for one concrete workflow, from which tools and AI agents can validate, compare, render, and hand off the design. | A versioned YAML design file, for example `solution.wds.yaml`, validated against a WDS schema. |
| 11 | Human-readable WDS views | Architecture diagrams, rationale, execution views, review material, and implementation handoff generated from or traceably aligned with the canonical WDS. | Markdown documents and diagrams generated from, or traceably linked to, the WDS YAML file. |
| 12 | Runtime mappings | Guidance that shows how a concrete workflow runtime or framework can provide the vendor-neutral capabilities and guarantees required by the RA, without making any product the standard. | A short `.md` guide or compatibility matrix for a workflow engine, agent runtime, or orchestration framework. It maps each RA requirement, such as durable wait, approval, state, retry, or safe external execution, to the platform capability that supports it and identifies what the implementation must still provide. |

### Consequence

The concepts selected by the WG become the next candidates to bring into the job-oriented RA foundation. Concepts not selected remain future possibilities; they are not rejected.

## How to vote

Feel free to reply with any kind of comment, but consider using following format for brevity: 

```text
Decision 1: <A or B>
Decision 2: <up to 3 numbers from the table, ie: 3, 6, 9>

Optional: another concept we should consider: <short description>

...additional comments...
```
